title: The Smell Of Rot In The Summer
author: William Saville
content:
The leaves rustled in the warm summer breeze, as the smell of rain wafted through the air.

The grass still clung to its morning dew, and the earth crumbled and rose from a nearby grave as fingers clawed at the topsoil.

Hours of labor passed, the sky was awash in the  technicolor of dusk, as he finally broke the surface with his face. He did not need to gasp for air, for his lungs had decayed. Eyes white and unseeing, limbs swinging, and teeth bared. He finally reached his goal of the surface, his tattered coffin far beneath him, ripped apart with fingers too strong. Raspy snarls surrounded him, for he was only one of many. The call of the necromancer has been heard in this graveyard of poor souls. Mindless machines made of rotted flesh, the shambling corpses started their walk towards their master deep in battle. Dew long gone from the grass, for too much time had passed, wetness replaced by bodily fluids that was thick like tar. He limped onward, creaking and moaning, ready to aid the one that had called him forth. But it was over before he got there, suddenly the magic that summoned him was gone, and he fell back to the ground. The necromancer, not understanding how long it takes a corpse to crawl from their grave, had summoned him and the others too late, and had died before they could come to his aid. With the necromancer's death, the spirit of the corpse, which looked on in disgust, exhaled an unneeded breath of air he had been holding. Returning to his eternal rest. For he no longer needed to watch with horror, as a spirit, while his unholy abomination of a corpse roamed the plains. Necromancers rarely think of the poor souls that must watch their bodies, souls ripped from rest. The ground was littered with rot, and the necromancer's own corpse was surrounded by the corpses he had disturbed for his own gains. Pity, that the necromancer would not be alive to appreciate the irony of it all.
